strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: validating neural posterior estimates, where existing diagnostics like SBC and TARP have significant limitations.
Provides a conformal calibration approach that yields finite-sample Type-I error control for any fixed classifier (Lemma 1), decoupling validity from classifier quality.

Theoretical analysis links conformal p-value distribution to AUC and total variation (Lemmas 2-3) and provides a robustness bound to density ratio estimation error (Theorem 1), giving insight into why weak classifiers can still yield signal.
Empirical results across multiple controlled perturbations and classifier degradation show improved power over standard C2ST and competitive performance against SBC/TARP.
Includes a high-dimensional manifold experiment and an ablation on calibration size, demonstrating practical behavior beyond simple Gaussian settings.
Practical finding that the simple uniform conformal test often outperforms the shared-calibration multiple test from prior work.
Code and training details are provided (though the URL is missing in the manuscript).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the conformal C2ST is a direct application of conformal prediction to the existing C2ST; the uniform test is a straightforward aggregation of conformal p-values with a KS test, overlapping substantially with Hu & Lei [1].

Theoretical guarantee is incomplete: Theorem 1 bounds the expected p-value difference under L2 estimation error, but does not directly bound the power of the KS test, and the bound can be vacuous if the classifier error is large, so the claim that 'weak classifiers' yield powerful tests is not fully justified.

Empirical evaluation is restricted to synthetic controlled perturbations (Gaussian and a synthetic manifold); no real-world NPE benchmarks or black-box simulators are included, making the 'wide range of benchmarks' and 'state of the art' claims overstated.

Computational cost: the uniform test requires m fresh samples from p for each test point, which can be prohibitive when the simulator p(y|θ) is expensive; the paper's assertion that p samples are cheap is questionable and conflicts with the black-box simulator setting.
Comparison with SBC and TARP may not be entirely fair, as they are not classifier-based and have different requirements; the robustness-to-classifier-degradation experiment cannot include them.
Presentation issues: several typos and confusing statements (e.g., 'does not require forward simulation through the generative model'), and the code URL is missing.
The method assumes a shared marginal π(y) and global validity, but does not address per-observation posterior validation or cases where y marginals differ.
The 'multiple test' adaptation has a complex variance estimate; its theoretical justification is only sketched, and its practical advantage over the uniform test is not clearly established.

strengths: The core proposal—using conformal calibration of classifier scores for the C2ST—is well-motivated and yields a clean finite-sample marginal validity guarantee (Lemma 1), which is a genuinely useful property that thresholded-accuracy C2ST lacks.

Lemma 2 and Lemma 3 provide an intuitive and correct link between the ranking quality of a scoring function (AUC) and the expected conformal p-value (E[U] = 1 - AUC), giving a principled rationale for why rank-based tests can extract signal from weak classifiers.

The empirical demonstration that conformal variants degrade far more gracefully than the thresholded C2ST as the classifier is degraded (Figure 2b and Appendix figures) is a real and interesting robustness phenomenon, and the translation/rotation toy example (Figure 1) cleanly isolates the effect.

The authors include an explicit limitations discussion and provide implementation details in the appendix, and they are transparent that the shared-calibration 'multiple test' variant is adapted from prior work.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim—that the conformal test retains 'non-trivial power that degrades gently' with classifier error—is not rigorously established. Theorem 1 only gives a one-sided bound on the mean p-value (E[Û] - E[U] ≤ O(ε^{2/3})) with an unspecified constant C depending on the (unknown) density of Z near zero. Because E[U] = 1/2 - TV/2, the bound is vacuous whenever TV/2 is smaller than the O(ε^{2/3}) term, and a bound on the mean p-value does not translate into any guarantee on the KS-based test's power (which depends on the full distribution of p-values). The promised 'power guarantee' is therefore asserted rather than proven.

Novelty is incremental. The method is a direct application of the conformal two-sample framework of Hu & Lei [1]; the 'uniform test' (fresh calibration set per test point + KS aggregation) is a straightforward construction, and Lemma 2 (density ratio maximizes AUC) is essentially Neyman–Pearson folklore. The genuinely new pieces (Lemma 3, Theorem 1) are relatively minor refinements, so the contribution is thin relative to the strong framing in the abstract and introduction.

The empirical evidence is entirely synthetic. All benchmarks use controlled Gaussian perturbations (NPTBench [16]) or a synthetic manifold flow; there is no experiment on a real simulator/NPE task (e.g., an actual trained NPE posterior on a non-trivial likelihood). This is a serious gap given the abstract's claim of 'state of the art performance for neural posterior evaluation across a wide range of benchmark problems.'

The comparisons are confounded by sample budget. Conformal Uniform(m) consumes up to m×1000 calibration samples from p (e.g., 200,000 for m=200), vastly more than the 1,000/2,000 samples used to train and evaluate C2ST. The reported power advantages may therefore reflect a much larger sampling budget rather than the conformal procedure itself, and no budget-matched control is provided.

Several claims are unsupported by the presented theory or experiments. The abstract asserts that 'overfit' classifiers can still yield reliable tests, yet no theory or experiment addresses overfitting specifically; the degradation study only simulates weak/underfit classifiers by linearly interpolating trained weights with randomly initialized weights, which is an artificial proxy that may not represent realistic weak classifiers.

Reproducibility and presentation are below standard. The code link is truncated ('The code is available at'), notation is inconsistent (m vs. k, n_q vs. n_g in Eq. 3, Appendix B.2 redefines k), and there are multiple typographical errors ('have have made', 'must therefore must be applied', 'the the ordinary C2ST'). Key quantities (the KS procedure, exact power computation, the constant in Theorem 1) are underspecified.

strengths: Introduces conformal calibration to the classifier two-sample test for neural posterior validation, with exact finite-sample Type-I error control via conformal p-values and a KS-based uniformity test.

Provides useful theoretical insights: Lemma 2 shows the density ratio maximizes AUC; Lemma 3 relates the expected conformal p-value to AUC and total variation; Theorem 1 bounds the degradation of the expected p-value under L2 error of the estimated density ratio.

Empirical results on controlled perturbed Gaussian benchmarks and a synthetic high-dimensional manifold show conformal variants are substantially more robust to classifier degradation than standard C2ST and competitive with SBC/TARP.

The core intuition—using score rankings rather than thresholded classifier accuracy—is appealing and well illustrated by the toy example, especially for translation perturbations that preserve rankings.
The limitations section honestly acknowledges the cheap-simulation assumption and the conservativeness of the theoretical bounds.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 only controls the mean of the conformal p-value, not the power of the KS test; it does not provide a finite-sample power guarantee, and the O(ε^{2/3}) bound is asymptotic in m and may be vacuous for large ε or very weak classifiers.

The empirical evaluation is limited to synthetic perturbed Gaussians and one synthetic manifold; no real scientific NPE benchmark tasks or actual trained NPE posteriors (e.g., SNPE, diffusion/flow-based NPE) are tested, so the claim of state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of benchmarks is overstated.

The uniform test requires an independent calibration set per test point, leading to m×n_q samples from p. Comparisons with C2ST may be confounded by a much larger sample budget for conformal uniform (e.g., m=200 uses 200,000 p samples vs. 1,000 for C2ST), and fairness is not fully controlled.

Reproducibility is weakened: the code link is missing ('The code is available at' with no URL), and key training details (batch size, activation, exact classifier output used, optimizer settings) are incomplete.

The classifier degradation experiment (linear interpolation with random initialization) may not reflect realistic weak classifiers, such as those underfitting due to limited data or overfitting; the abstract's mention of overfit classifiers is not empirically tested.

The theoretical robustness result relies on Assumption 2 (L2 error of the density ratio), which may not hold for very weak classifiers, and the paper does not discuss how to verify or achieve this condition in practice.
The multiple test variant is adapted from prior work with minimal new analysis; its asymptotic validity and power in the NPE setting are not thoroughly examined or calibrated empirically.

strengths: Provides a principled conformal framework for two-sample testing in NPE validation, with exact finite-sample validity for the uniform test and asymptotic validity for the budget-matched multiple test.
Theoretical robustness analysis (Theorem 3.5, 4.2) quantifies graceful degradation in terms of classifier estimation error, showing O(ε^{2/3}) dependence, which is a useful new understanding.

Empirical evaluation is extensive: controlled Gaussian perturbations, CIFAR-10 corruptions, and a gravitational-lensing benchmark; includes many baselines (C2ST, SBC, TARP, DC, AutoML, MMDFuse) and stress-tests classifier degradation.
Demonstrates that ranking quality (AUC) rather than classification accuracy drives power, and that conformal methods are more robust to weak classifiers than standard C2ST.
Reproducibility: code available, detailed hyperparameters, multiple seeds/replicates, and an honest limitations section.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core conformal two-sample test is from Hu & Lei (2024), and the paper itself notes their tests are a special case. The main new contribution is the robustness analysis and NPE application, which is incremental.

Overclaiming in title/abstract: 'Turning weak classifiers into strong two-sample tests' and 'exact, finite-sample p-values' for both variants. The multiple test is only asymptotically valid (acknowledged in limitations), and a truly weak (random) classifier yields no power. The title overstates the method's ability.

The uniform test requires mN extra samples from the true joint p, which in many NPE applications involves expensive simulator calls; the paper's budget comparison (Table 1) frames q-sampling as costly, which is often backwards since q is the cheap learned posterior. The limitations acknowledge this, but the main text presentation is misleading.

Theoretical robustness assumes a bounded MSE for the density-ratio estimate \hat r, which may be large for weak classifiers; the O(ε^{2/3}) bound is not directly a power guarantee and may be loose. The analysis does not directly bound test power under weak classifiers.

Some technical assumptions are ambiguous or strong (e.g., Assumption 4.1's 'ties occur at rate O_p(1)'; Assumption 3.4's low-noise condition), and the multiple test's finite-sample behavior is not established.
The test is global and does not localize mismatches; this is acknowledged but limits practical utility for debugging NPE models.

The baseline DC is reported as invalid due to Type-I inflation; while this may be true, the paper does not fully investigate whether this is due to its adaptation or inherent, and stronger scrutiny would be helpful.

strengths: Genuine finite-sample Type-I validity for the uniform variant: Lemma 3.1 gives marginal uniformity of each conformal p-value for any deterministic score, and aggregating i.i.d. p-values with a KS test yields valid (exact/asymptotic) Type-I control. This is a real and useful guarantee that standard C2ST only has asymptotically.

The robustness analysis (Theorem 3.5, Theorem 4.2) is a reasonable extension of Hu & Lei (2024): relating the density-ratio estimation error (L2 <= epsilon^2) to the deviation of conformal p-values via a Tsybakov-type margin condition (Assumption 3.4) with an O(epsilon^{2/3}) rate. The proofs (Appendix A.2, A.4) appear correct on inspection.

The budget-matched multiple test is a practically valuable contribution: it reuses a single shared calibration set to match C2ST's simulation cost while empirically retaining more power, which is directly useful for expensive simulators.
Timely and relevant application to NPE validation, addressing documented limitations of rank-SBC (marginal-only, multiple testing) and TARP (proposal sensitivity) with a joint-distribution test.

Broad empirical coverage: controlled Gaussian perturbations, CIFAR-10 corruption, a gravitational-lensing inverse problem, and manifold-structured posteriors, with a clear budget accounting (Table 1).
weaknesses: Limited methodological originality: the authors themselves state their tests 'appear as a special case of' Hu & Lei (2024). The only method-level additions are the fresh-calibration-per-point + KS aggregation and the robustness analysis; the multiple test is an adaptation of Hu & Lei's U-statistic.

The central 'power' claim is not rigorously established by the theory. Theorem 3.5 bounds the difference in expected p-values (E[Uhat]-E[U]) and Theorem 4.2 bounds a relative statistic gap; neither directly bounds the test's power (e.g., the KS sup-deviation or rejection probability). The link from E[U] to power is heuristic, so the headline claim that weak classifiers yield powerful tests rests mainly on the (controlled) experiments.

The toy translation experiment (Fig. 1b) is close to trivial: for a linear signed-distance score, translating the boundary is a constant shift, which leaves ranks unchanged, so exact rank-invariance of the conformal test is guaranteed by construction. This is presented as evidence of 'robustness to biased classifiers' but demonstrates little beyond the monotone-transform invariance already stated.

Baseline fairness is questionable. DC (Yao & Domke, 2023), a published method, is reported to fail Type-I control and is deemed 'invalid'; with m=10 and 2000 epochs this may reflect misconfiguration rather than a genuine property of DC. Strong conclusions ('state of the art') drawn against a possibly broken baseline weaken the empirical case.

The uniform test's power advantage is partly an artifact of using m-times more samples from p (Table 1), so it is not budget-matched; the fairer comparison (multiple test) is relegated to a smaller role and its gains are more modest in some regimes (e.g., Table 2b, beta >= 0.9).

Overstated framing: the title/abstract ('turning weak classifiers into strong two-sample tests') is undercut by the acknowledged 'hard floor' that power requires AUC > 0.5; a weak classifier that destroys the ranking cannot be rescued, so the contribution is a robustness/calibration result rather than a transformation of arbitrary weak classifiers.

Presentation issues: main-text experiments rely heavily on the appendix, several main-text figures (2, 3, 6-11) are hard to read, and the code URL is left dangling ('available at'), which matters for reproducibility.

strengths: Targets an important and timely problem: validating Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) posteriors, where existing diagnostics (SBC, TARP, DC) have well-documented weaknesses (marginal-only sensitivity, proposal-dependence, Type-I inflation).

Provides a coherent theoretical story: exact finite-sample Type-I control for the uniform test (Lemma 3.1), an AUC-based characterization of power (Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3), and robustness-to-estimation-error guarantees for weak classifiers (Theorem 3.5 and Theorem 4.2) with graceful O(eps^{2/3}) degradation. The AUC/ranking perspective gives a clean operational account of when the test works.

Two complementary variants with a clearly articulated budget/power trade-off: the uniform test (finite-sample valid, needs mN draws from the cheap p side) and the budget-matched multiple test (asymptotically valid, matches C2ST cost). The practitioner's guide in Appendix D is genuinely useful.

Extensive and mostly convincing empirical evaluation: controlled Gaussian perturbations (four in the main text, more in appendix), CIFAR-10 corruption experiments, and a real gravitational-lensing inverse problem, with a systematic classifier-degradation (beta-interpolation) stress test showing large robustness advantages over C2ST, AutoML, SBC, TARP, and MMDFuse.

Honest and thorough limitations section, reproducibility details (architectures, training, sample budgets, seeds, replicate counts), and an impact statement. The paper is candid that its tests specialize Hu and Lei (2024) and that power is capped by ranking quality.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty relative to Hu and Lei (2024). The authors themselves state their tests 'appear as a special case of theirs.' The central new theory (Theorem 3.5 and Theorem 4.2) is built on largely inherited machinery (conformal p-values, the U-statistic Hoeffding decomposition/CLT from Hu and Lei), and the O(eps^{2/3}) rate is obtained by optimizing a somewhat loose bound (E[|Z|1{|Z|<=t}] <= Ct^2 plus a Markov/Cauchy-Schwarz term); no tightness or matching lower bound is shown, so the practical sharpness of the rate is unclear.

A key baseline that would isolate the contribution is missing. The multiple test is essentially a rank-based (Mann-Whitney/AUC-style) test on the classifier score, so much of the gain over C2ST could stem from using continuous ranks instead of 0/1 thresholding rather than from 'conformal calibration' per se. A direct comparison against a plain rank-sum test on the same classifier scores is needed to substantiate the framing.

The headline claim of 'turning weak classifiers into strong two-sample tests' is somewhat oversold. Power is fundamentally bounded by the classifier's AUC (acknowledged as a 'hard floor'), and a truly random classifier (beta ~ 1) yields no power (Fig. 2b, Table 2b). The toy translation example is almost trivially robust because any monotone score of theta still perfectly separates the shifted Gaussians, which may give an overly optimistic impression of robustness.

The power comparisons are not budget-matched in Fig. 2a: the uniform test uses mN draws from p (m up to 50), a far larger budget than the baselines, which complicates head-to-head interpretation even though the cost asymmetry is disclosed in Table 1. The strongest fair comparison (Conformal Multiple at matched budget) is only shown for some settings.

Presentation issues: main-text figures are low-resolution and hard to read in places; the code link is truncated ('The code is available at'); the uniform test's requirement of an independent fresh calibration set per test point is a non-trivial implementation detail that could be easy to misuse.
